description:
Danish astronomer at the Royal Observatory in Paris

Romer noticed that eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io ran early when Earth was closest to Jupiter, and late when it was furthest away. The gap was not Io's orbit changing: it was extra light needing extra distance to cross. Most scientists at the time assumed light travelled instantly.

how long Romer calculated light takes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit around the Sun.

His figures imply a speed of about 226,663 kilometres per second: roughly 24% slower than the true value of 299,792 km/s. He was off by a quarter. He was also the first person in history to prove light has a speed at all.

Giovanni Cassini, the observatory's own director and the astronomer whose data Romer had used, never fully accepted the theory. It won support elsewhere in Europe well before Paris came around to it.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%B8mer%27s_determination_of_the_speed_of_light: confirms Ole Romer, working at the Royal Observatory in Paris, demonstrated in 1676 that light has a finite, measurable speed by timing eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io; that he estimated light takes about 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit; that this implies a speed of about 226,663 km/s, 24.4% lower than the true value of 299,792 km/s; and that Giovanni Domenico Cassini, the observatory's director, never fully accepted the theory even though it gained wider acceptance elsewhere.
